lesson_title: Find the Fire: Climbing the Atmosphere's Four Layers
hook_text: The sky is a mountain with campfires in all the wrong places.
clip_script: Climb a mountain that does not exist, four camps high, where the fires burn in all the wrong places. Base camp is the troposphere, and its fire is the ground you stand on: the earth soaks up sunshine and breathes the warmth back out, so every step you climb takes you deeper into cold. That is why Matroosberg carries snow while Paarl, down the valley, is picnic weather. Camp two is the stratosphere — someone hung the fire above the camp: ozone near the tent roof catches ultraviolet and glows warm, so climbing gets warmer. Warm air on cold air is a lid — nothing stirs, no cloud forms, and that is why airliners cruise there. Camp three, the mesosphere, has no fire at all: the coldest roof on the mountain, around minus ninety, where space gravel burns into shooting stars. The summit is the thermosphere: thousands of degrees on the thermometer, and you would still freeze, because almost no molecules remain to hand you the heat. Four camps. Down, up, down, up.
visual_style: A stylised mountain in cross-section with four glowing campfires appearing in impossible positions, a thin climber silhouette ascending, and a zigzag temperature line tracing itself beside the slope.
mood: Adventurous and a little surreal, ending in quiet wonder.
pacing: One steady beat per camp, tightening toward the summit, final hard landing on 'down, up, down, up'.
call_to_action: Take the full lesson and redraw the atmosphere's temperature graph from memory — no heights required.
